data.title: Veľký Tríbeč – a vast prehistoric hillfort
data.excerpt: On the highest peak of the Tríbeč range, a single rampart 1,882 m long encloses 102 hectares — a fortification of enormous extent even among the hillforts of the Lusatian culture. Described by Odescalchi in 1922 and surveyed in detail by Štefan Janšák in 1929, it was apparently looted by metal detectorists during the 1990s; the systematic investigation of 2024 has now changed what we know about its dating.

timeline.title: The hillfort is built and mainly used
timeline.description: Pottery finds from the Early Iron Age (the Hallstatt period), sherds dated to the Final Bronze Age and the Hallstatt period, and finds of the Lusatian culture at the end of the Bronze Age connect the main use of this massive hillfort with the people of the Lusatian culture and with the Hallstatt period.

timeline.title: The hillfort is used again
timeline.description: After the end of the Lusatian culture the hillfort was apparently abandoned for a time; several centuries later people used it again in the La Tène and Roman periods, though not in the original extent of the fortification, only in the more suitable smaller parts.

children.text: The Tríbeč range is known not only for legends about people who vanish mysteriously, but also for its rich history. It is dotted with a network of extensive fortifications from the Final Bronze Age, and from other periods as well. Among the best-known hillforts of Tríbeč are Žibrica, Veľký and Malý Lysec, Zobor and Veľký Tríbeč. And it is the last of these that the following lines are devoted to.

Getting there

The Veľký Tríbeč hillfort can be reached from several directions along waymarked trails. The red Ponitrie long-distance trail passes through it, and you can join that trail either at Zlatno or at Kostoľany pod Tribečom. From the west a blue waymarked trail leads up to the hillfort from Kovarce, and from the north another one from Solčany. On the summit of the hillfort, which is not overgrown with trees, you can rest and eat the supplies you have brought with you in the lap of nature.
The history of research

The first person to describe and draw the hillfort was Lívius Odescalchi, a large landowner at Solčany, who submitted his manuscript to the Anthropological Society in Vienna; the paper was subsequently published in German in full in the society's annual report in 1922, together with 5 illustrations in the text.

At a later date, a surviving manuscript of an eleven-page study entitled “O prähistorickom pevnostnom vale na vrchu Tríbči” (On the prehistoric fortification rampart on the hill of Tríbeč) from the beginning of the 20th century, which gives no author, was discovered in the Matica archive in Martin. In his paper entitled “O autorstve rukopisu o predhistorickom obrannom vale na vrchu Tribeč” (On the authorship of the manuscript about the prehistoric defensive rampart on the hill of Tribeč), the botanist Pavol Eliáš demonstrated quite convincingly that this text is practically only a Slovak translation of the above-mentioned German paper by Odescalchi. In the paper he states, for example, that

“In the stone rampart there were four openings – gates 8 to 10 metres wide. At each gate there was a recess of 10 to 30 metres, forming a protective bastion. Four roads led to the hillfort – one to the south towards Velčice, three to the north towards Solčany.”

Besides this interesting description of the hillfort, the original paper also contains a drawing of the site from the beginning of the 20th century, from which it is clearly visible where the original gates into the hillfort lay within the circuit of the fortification. In later times the rampart of the hillfort was cut through artificially in several places for various reasons (probably timber extraction and the like).

children.text: The next scholar to take an interest in the hillfort was our old acquaintance, the legendary Štefan Janšák, who described and drew the site in detail. Let us therefore give the floor to this bard of Slovak archaeology, in his paper of 1929:

The hillfort of Veľký Tribeč lies on the summit of the mountain of the same name, which rises in the south-western belt of the Nitra hills to an altitude of 820 m. The dominant position held by the hillforts on Zobor and Zubrica is heightened here still further. Admittedly, to its own detriment, and to the disadvantage of the practicality and comfort of its ancient inhabitants, there is the excessive distance from water, from fertile plains and from suitable routes, a factor which made itself felt in the construction of the hillfort. One cannot, however, deny Veľký Tríbeč a robust and rugged massiveness, which is increased still more by the wild, so-called untouched nature around it, in fact a half-primeval forest. Veľký Tribeč is the highest domed peak of the main ridge of the Nitra hills, a peak which on the north-eastern side rises barely 60 m above the ridge, but on the south-western side falls away in a great step of 450 m, by which the continuous ridge is in fact interrupted. Through this geographical formation Veľký Tribeč approaches a mountain promontory running out into the plain. Since, however, its gradient is not steep enough and the mountain retains the shape of a cone with a domed top, the hillfort that came into being on Veľký Tríbeč belongs to the second category. The geological formation of the summit of Veľký Tribeč and of the nearest slope within a radius of 3–6 km is good granite, little subject to weathering. Veľký Tribeč ends below the spot height of 829 m on the south-western side in a low granite crag. The natural security of the hillfort consists perhaps solely in the fact that it is too far from the plain, in the middle of dense forest, in a tangle of crossing gullies and subsidiary ridges, and is therefore hard to find. Only on the north, north-eastern and eastern sides is the natural step in the terrain to some extent steeper, and that decidedly to the benefit of security.

blocks.alt: Veľký Tríbeč – a vast prehistoric hillfort

children.text: The fortification of the hillfort consists of a single rampart, whose course is apparent from the plan. Between the highest point of the hillfort (820) and the lowest (730) there is a difference of 90 m, which in no way contributes to its security. On the eastern side, from which access is fairly comfortable and easy, the inhabitants of the hillfort built an auxiliary rampart, later interrupted by a road built for hauling timber. The total length of the circuit rampart amounts to 1,882 m, that of the auxiliary rampart to 200 m. Its height towards the interior of the hillfort ranges from 0.5 to 1 m. On the outside the rampart merges with the natural fall of the ground, thus forming a step 4 to 5 m high. The material used for its construction was obtained on the spot and shows no traces of fire, nor does it contain any other finds. The main entrance, secured in the direction of the road by prolonged ramparts (a blocking work, analogous to the one at Zobor), lies on the north-western side and appears to be the only original entrance. The others, at least, of which there are several, lack such a blocking work. The area of the hillfort amounts to 102 ha and in its quality (with regard to the purpose pursued by the original inhabitants) it is almost everywhere of equal value, showing no gradation in quality. The extensive slope inclined to the south is indeed protected against northerly winds, but offers no particular security in case defence became necessary. The security of the highest summit and of the plateau extending from it towards the north-east consists solely in their elevation above the surroundings and in their distance from the ramparts, which would take the first impact. On Veľký Tribeč there are no remains of dwellings, refuges or cisterns serving the needs of its earliest inhabitants. On the summit there are abundant finds of small potsherds from the first Iron Age (the Hallstatt period)

children.text: After Janšák, essentially nobody devoted any more detailed research to the hillfort, and the site was left at the mercy of illegal metal detectorists who, as at other hillforts, saw to the looting of the larger metal objects in particular, apparently already during the 1990s. In 2001 the archaeologists Jana Katkinová and Slavomír Katkin carried out only a surface collection at the hillfort and published the results of their survey in the AVANS yearbook for 2001. They found only a few diagnostic sherds, which they dated broadly, like Janšák, to the Final Bronze Age and the Hallstatt period. The archaeologists Borza and Borzová also studied the hillfort on the basis of aerial photography in 2019, although they carried out neither classical test trenching nor collection there. Even so, their paper brings interesting information about the course of the fortification and about the outlying rampart. In September 2024 an investigation of the hillfort was carried out by the Monuments Board of the Slovak Republic (Peter Bisták, Petra Kmeťová, Martin Neumann) and the Regional Monuments Board in Nitra (Michal Gróf), with the contribution of our civic association Hradiská and of Archeo Moravia; the hillfort was investigated systematically and with the help of a metal detector. One of the foundations of the work was high-quality modern lidar survey of the terrain.

blocks.alt: Veľký Tríbeč – a vast prehistoric hillfort

children.text: The 2024 investigation

The results of the archaeological investigation in 2024 surprised all of us and brought entirely new insights into the dating of the hillfort, as well as a number of unexpected finds (for example small fragments of bronze objects from the Late and Final Bronze Age, metal casting lumps and fragments of brooches), which we trust will soon be studied and published by specialists so that we can share them with our readers. At this stage we have been given permission to publish a few of them. Besides these you can also see a clay spindle whorl and several potsherds, dated apparently to the period of the Lusatian culture at the end of the Bronze Age. Perhaps I may reveal at least this much: the investigation on Veľký Tríbeč too has shown that the enormous Lusatian/Hallstatt hillforts were apparently abandoned for a time after the end of the Lusatian culture, and that after several centuries people used them again in the La Tène and Roman periods — though not in the original extent of the fortification; rather, they tended to use only the more suitable smaller parts of the hillfort. The same trend can be seen at other originally Hallstatt-period extensive hillforts, for example Holíš, Udiča-Hradište, Marhát and many others. It will probably be connected with the fact that in later periods the hillforts were inhabited by smaller groups of people, who would not have been able to defend a fortification as enormous as the original circuit.
